title: Fast 50 Growth Is Slowing. Which Bids Are Still Worth Chasing?
summary: When growth slows, contractors gain an advantage by declining weak bids quickly and choosing the right teaming partners.
body_markdown:
## What the 2026 Fast 50 Shows


Growth slowed in 2025 among the fastest-growing small contractors. Washington Technology’s 2026 Fast 50 ranks small businesses by their compound annual growth rate (CAGR) from 2021 through 2025. Of the 50 companies, 36 grew more slowly from 2024 to 2025 than their respective averages over the prior three years, and 12 had revenue declines. The No. 1 firm, Makwa Global, claimed the top spot again with a 109.4% CAGR, down from 251.8% the year before.


Growth also varied by line of business. The article reports that high-tech firms on the list grew at a median 40% CAGR, against 24% for IT services firms. It points to policy changes from the current presidential administration and cuts from the Department of Government Efficiency as context for the slowdown.


Washington Technology describes the slowdown as common across the market, as a slowdown among the leaders is a reasonable signal to tighten how you spend your capture and proposal budget.


## Why does a slowdown change how you should bid?


Every lost bid costs more when growth is harder to find. Proposal dollars, senior time and capture attention don’t come back after a loss.


Many contractors respond by bidding on more opportunities to make up the difference. But bidding on more opportunities can have the opposite of the desired effect. More bids spread a fixed budget thinner and can lower your win rate on the bids that matter.


## What does it mean to be critical of your pipeline?


A critical pipeline review ranks the pipeline as a set of investments, not keeping every opportunity alive. The core measure is probability of win, or pWin: your estimated chance of winning a specific opportunity, often expressed as a percentage or as high, medium or low. An honest pWin reflects the evidence, not how much you want the work. Capture practitioners also warn that raw scores tend to run optimistic, so pressure-test yours.


We recommend asking the following questions in a pipeline review:


1. **Did you help shape this opportunity, or did you first see it when it posted?** Seeing an RFP for the first time at release often means competitors saw it first.
2. **Do you know the customer’s real problem, in their words?** If your understanding comes only from the solicitation, your pWin is a guess.
3. **Is there an incumbent, and is the customer satisfied?** A well-regarded incumbent is hard to displace.
4. **Does the evaluation scheme favor your strengths?** A lowest price technically acceptable (LPTA) evaluation favors the lowest-priced compliant offer, while a best-value tradeoff can reward a stronger technical approach.
5. **Does your past performance map to the scope, size and agency?** The agency decides which past performance is relevant, and GAO generally defers to that judgment unless it is unreasonable.
6. **Are your teammates identified and their terms agreed early?** Late teaming rarely produces a strong team.


## Screens For a Fast Bid/No-Bid Decision


A fast bid/no-bid decision weighs whether you can win the opportunity and whether you should sign the contract if you win it.


The win-probability screen comes first so that legal and finance time goes only to bids you have a realistic chance of winning. Score each row green or red, and decide in advance how many reds mean no-bid.


Win-probability signal Green Red


Customer relationship Direct contact, shaped requirements First contact was the RFP


Competitive position A discriminator you can prove Entrenched incumbent, no discriminator


Team Teaming terms agreed early Teaming still open at release


Capability fit Past performance maps to scope Stretch on scope, size or agency


Cost to pursue Fits capture and proposal budget Consumes budget better bids need


The second check is the contract-term risk screen from “Planning for a Divided Government: Contract Terms to Check Now” (General Legal, Nov. 13, 2026). That post lays out a seven-row green/red screen that covers funding, stop-work and termination, payment trigger, options, subcontractors, data rights and IP, and strategic fit.


Set a threshold for each screen. A bid that fails the win-probability screen is a no-bid. A bid that fails the contract-term screen goes to legal review or is a no-bid. A bid can score well on win probability and still carry terms you cannot accept. A clean contract is no reason to chase a bid you are unlikely to win.


The two screens look at cost from different angles. “Cost to pursue” in the first screen asks whether the pursuit fits your capture and proposal budget. The options row in the second asks whether the base period recovers your bid and startup cost. Most teams set an internal threshold below which they don’t bid, unless there is a strategic reason. In the Nov. 13 post, strategic fit means work you would invest in under all three funding scenarios it describes, and we would apply the same test here. Decide within a few days and document your reasoning, creating a record to tune your scoring over time. Each no-bid frees budget and staff time for the bids you are more likely to win.


## Investments That Improve pWin


Investments that improve evaluation scores include customer engagement before the RFP, teammates with complementary past performance, and a proposal built around a discriminator evaluators can verify. Spend less polishing bids where the fundamentals aren’t there.


## Why might a slower market mean more teaming, JVs and M&A?


When organic growth slows, companies look elsewhere for capability, past performance and set-aside eligibility. That could mean a teaming arrangement for one bid, a joint venture for a larger vehicle, or an acquisition.


These deals requiring legal work tend to land when capture and operations teams are already stretched.


Timing creates the main practical risk. A strong teammate may move on while the agreement is still under negotiation. But rushing creates its own problems, because a hastily drafted agreement can leave problems like unclear exclusivity, open-ended work-share commitments, vague IP and data rights, or terms that don’t match what the prime flows down later.


## Next Steps for Your Pipeline and Agreements


Contractors should first run a pipeline review this quarter using both screens and drop anything that fails either one against your written thresholds. Second, standardize the agreements you sign repeatedly, so a good teammate isn’t left waiting. Third, decide in advance which deal terms are fixed and which you will trade.

FAQs


### Is the slowdown limited to the smallest firms?


The data covers the 50 fastest-growing small businesses, and 36 of them grew more slowly from 2024 to 2025 than in the prior three years. However, a slowdown among the fastest-growing firms likely indicates tighter conditions across the rest of the market, and Washington Technology describes the pattern as common market-wide.


### Should I bid on more opportunities to offset slower growth?


In most cases, bidding on more opportunities does not offset slower growth. More low-pWin bids spread a fixed budget thinner. Fewer, better-chosen bids tend to protect both budget and win rate.


### What is pWin?


pWin is your estimated probability of winning a specific opportunity, based on customer knowledge, competition, fit and team strength.
